They have alienated one party and have not acquired any sure hold upon the other. Between 1864 and 1866, while preparing thesis for graduation, I obtained statistics on the general subject of the relation of occupation to health and longevity that convinced me of the error of the accepted teachings in regard to the effect of mental labor. The views I then advocated, and which I enforced by statistical evidence, were:

1. That the brain-working classes—clergymen, lawyers, physicians, merchants, scientists and men of letters—lived very much longer than the muscle-working classes.

2. That those who followed occupations that called both muscle and brain into exercise were longer lived than those who lived in occupations that were purely manual.

ANDREW Thomas, one of the most beloved citizens of Hinds county, died at his residence, near Bolton, on the inst., in the 80th year of his age.

Born in the State of North Carolina, he migrated to the State of Mississippi about as near as fifty years ago. He was one of a numerous siz of brothers, all of whom, except one, died in this county for many years.

Old citizens still cherish remembrance of them, the oldest of the family being Thomas, who long held the office of [?] Gan Office at present so well filled by his worthy, excellent and patriotic son, S. B. Thomas, and who was affectionately regarded by the younger men of his day.

The subject of this obituary was distinguished in equal degree—indeed, was the watermark of his elder brother, in integrity of life and character, fidelity, friendship and charity to all mankind. They were beloved in their day and generation, and both died, it is believed, without leaving an enemy behind. Their purses, in their hands, were open as day, to the needs of the widow and the orphan. The helpless and distressed were never turned away empty from their hospitable abodes—and sons of toil, early life struggling with adverse fortune, without influential friends, they rose to independence, and commanded the respect and esteem of all who knew them.

The very struggles, with the self-denials and sacrifices they imposed, instead of toughening their hearts, melted them in sympathy for all who were called to travel the same rugged and thorny road. So more simple-minded, pure-hearted, serious, hospitable, benevolent men, the friends and patrons of his own struggles, now more than forty years ago, and he is able, from his own personal experience, to testify of the noble virtues that adorned their characters. Whilst one of them passed to his rest, as we know, in the bosom of his Heavenly Father,

They had twenty-three years ago, they so strikingly identified, when both were living, that we cannot separate them, as both are dead. The Siamese were not more closely and indissolubly connected by adhesive ligaments than were brothers, David and Andrew Thomas.

What was most striking or marked CHARACTER of the one, was equally evident in the character of the other. So, only two years in age they were upon the journey of life, and in connection between them was more still! by the fact that, in early life, they married sisters, lived near each other. The two families mingled as if they were the same family.

No words might exhaust itself, and fail to praise them in their domestic relations; these were all that heart could say.

Andrew Thomas departed this life in the peace and communion of the Baptist Church, in which he had long been a member, with full assurance of blessedness beyond the grave.

A FRIEND.

moval to Meridian, the floor of the plating
room was taken up, burned, and the ashes
analysed, with the result of procuring
pure silver to the amount of 1881. This
result is not so strange—appears at first
sight. The precious metals are capable
of extreme rehabilitation under heat, be-
coming mere vapors, which may be con-
densed, resulting in the production of the
metal in pure form. But, even without
heat, the particles of gold and silver are
made so exceedingly fine, in the process
of the manufacture of gold and silver
goods, whether solid or plated, that no
device can salvage the material afterwards.

He was a tall, lank man, with a shrewd, cunning face, clothed with one of those perpetual smiles which it would be relief to see broken now and then by a frown.


"Show Mr. Clavering up, Leech," said he to one of my friends, "you know the way, and have a word to say to brother Pellet here."


Leech took my arm, and at the end of a long hallway on the third floor, led me into a dimly lighted room. I thought it a strange place to conduct a guest to, but made no remark.


"Be seated," said Leech—"I shall return in a moment."


With that saying he stepped out and closed the door.


Though it was summer the night air was keen in that mountain region, and morning and evening fires were customary. Feeling a little chilly after our long ride, I attempted to draw a chair which stood near the wall toward the heating apparatus at one end of the room.


I was surprised to find the chair uncomfortable. My curiosity was excited. The lamp by which it was lighted hung from the ceiling out of reach. The only articles of furniture were the stationary chair, a small iron bedstead and bedding, the former fastened to the wall—and a wash-stand similarly secured. I examined the window. It was narrow and guarded outside by thick iron bars.
"What could be the meaning of all this?" I began to feel a tremor coming over me. Beads of perspiration stood on my forehead. I ran to the door, essayed to open it, but found it locked from without. I shook it violently, called loudly for Leech, and then made desperate efforts to kick down the door; but it was too strong and heavy, and inspection revealed the fact that it was thickly plated with iron.


A vague feeling of terror had almost seized me, when a noise attracted my attention. A portion of the door turned outward, as if upon a hinge, disclosing a small, square aperture, through which I discerned the face of Dr. Crochet, with a rigid, sickening smile.
"What is the meaning of this?" I demanded fiercely.


"Come, come, Mr. Clavering, be calm," said the doctor, in his smooth, hypocritical tone; "excitement will do you great harm, you see. We trust you will soon be better."


"Better!" exclaimed I—"why, there's nothing on earth the matter with me!"
"You are scarcely the best judge of that," was the quiet response.


"But I tell you I was never sick in my life!" yelled I, driven to frenzy by such insolent mockery.


"Not exactly sick, perhaps," returned the imperturbable doctor, "but you have not been quite yourself lately, you see—not quite," and he tapped my forehead significantly.


"Then you take me to be crazy?" I said, bursting into a laugh at the absurdity of the idea.


"Well, well, if you only keep quiet, and avoid excitement, we hope to bring you around in a month or so."

LOUISVILLE. Sept. 15.—The President's reception was continued to-day, and as upon the preceding occasion, was marked with the warmest welcome. After breakfast the party was escorted to the Female high school, and a march of welcome by the pupils greeted the PRESIDENT upon his appearance. All the members of the cabinet except Secretary Schurtz, who has left, and Attorney General Devens, who did not come to Louisville, were present, as were Misses Evarts and Mrs. Hayes and Coz.

The principal, Mr. Chase, in introducing the President to the scholars, made some delicate and complimentary illusions to Mrs. Hayes. Miss Florence White, of the senior class, welcomed the President in behalf of the pupils, presenting him with a magnificent bouquet of flowers, representing the American colors. The President said only a few words, and introduced Secretary Evarts, who compared the Northern and Southern educational advantages in favor of the latter. Secretary McCrary seconded these remarks and expressed his belief in the future of the State and city. Secretary Thompson, on being introduced, was heartily cheered. Another cheer was added, when Mr. Chase announced that he was an Indianan, and prolonged applause followed the Secretary's announcement that he began life as a school teacher. He then spoke on the importance of education. Judge Key made a pleasant address.

The central colored school was next visited and colored men welcomed the party. School exercises followed. In leaving, the President expressed qualification at the evidence of the liberal sentiment of Louisville on the subject of universal education. The carriages drove to the Third Ward school and thence to the blind asylum, where the inmates were singing a welcome chorus. They followed out the exercises indicated on raised letter programmes, at the conclusion of which the President, Secretary Evarts, Secretary McCrary and General Key made appropriate addresses. The President and party leave early to-morrow morning for Nashville. A number of journalists and Kentuckians accompany them.

In the afternoon the party proceeded to Jeffersonville, where they were handsomely entertained, after which they returned to Louisville. The farewell, taken in the vicinity of the exposition building, was one of decorative splendor. WADE HAMPTON, Dec.

CHEYENNE, w. T., Sept. 49,
The eastward bound passenger
train which passed here at 3 o.
m. to-day was stopped and rob-
bed by thirteen masked men at
Big Spring, Nebraska, 100 miles
east of this city tonight. The
robbers first took possession of
the station at the Springs, de-
stroyed the telegraph instru-
ments and compelled the agent
to hang out red light. When
the train stopped they boarded
it and placed the train men and
passengers under guard. The
express car was broken open
and the safe robbed of about
$4,000. The passengers here
were also robbed but their losses
are not yet known.

THE WINNERS RECEIVING THE PRIZES—THE BANQUET.


The formal presentation of the trophies of the International and Interstate rifle contests took place last evening at Gilmore's Garden, before a large assemblage. Every part of the garden was filled almost to overflowing, and it is thought there were less than a thousand people present. The first rustic box to the right of the entrance was devoted to the British team. Accompanying the members were Mrs. Col. Fenton, Mrs. Armitage, Mrs. Humphrey and the officers of the National Rifle Association. Folds of the jack and the British coat of arms were the distinctive decorations here while at the adjoining box the stars and stripes in graceful abundance showed where the American team gathered. The New Orleans and California gentlemen were seated on the opposite side of the entrance. Mr. Gilmore provided an abundance of appropriate music but for the majority of the assemblage, their eyes were more interested than their ears. At half-past nine the gentlemen formed in procession and marched to the music platform, being received along the line with unceasing cheers and waving of handkerchiefs and hats. When Sir Henry Halford, who made the speech of the evening, referred gracefully to his defeat, a loud voice shouted "Don't mention it," and there were other good-humored breaches of decorum.


Judge P. Stanton, President of the National Rifle Association, made the opening address. Judge Gilder sleeve spoke appropriately of the contests for the Times prize and those present of the winners. Mr. Bycnburgh, whom he described "small in stature but very large in shooting capacity," being received with great applause. Col. Wm. C. Church spoke to the subject "The Interstate Trophy." Judge John R. Brady spoke in a humorous vein of the International Trophy (which had settled in the folds of the Star-spangled Banner for a whole year and would nestle there another"). He then presented the trophy medals to the members of the American team, each victor he came forward being received with long and vociferous applause.

But the enthusiasm of the crowd knew bounds when Sir Henry Halford, Captain of the British team, was introduced. After waiting for two minutes he began in far-reaching tones which hushed the wild applause. His remarks were exceedingly apt and graceful, and in them some advice given by gentlemen at the range a few days ago when he had lost a prize, which seems to be opportune now, he said he had holding to "pay up and shut up." His presence here shows that I am not ashamed to pay up, but the question of shutting up is very different and I am not in the habit of taking defeat without trying to retrieve it. Judge Brady said a moment ago, talking about weeping, wailing and gnashing of teeth, "I will say I will set my teeth to win the victory." Judge Brady also remarked that America had sufficient victory over the British nation. "That you have beaten us cannot be questioned. You have done so honestly and fairly and we have realized that the proficiency we were satisfied with at home is score as we made was never before equaled but it was not enough to beat you. When we had it, we had it. But we would not take the prize from you. You won. You have shown your capability to meet the most proficient marksmen of the world. We have much to learn; he said, my say, we may be able in the future to compete with you again for the International trophy. There is but one drawback in which the warm hearts of Americans could show; but it is a drawback to our visit and that is, which you as a nation have shown to all of us. [Cheers] A tribute large on behalf of the Ladies of New-York" was presented. Capt. L. C. Bruce of the American team made the finest score, followed by the scores of members of the British team, who were each loudly cheered. Mr. Milner and others were loudly called upon and Rule Britannia was played while the procession returned to the boxes.


The winning teams and the members of the Crescent City and California teams attended a banquet given by the National Rifle Association directors. The affair was wholly informal, and several ladies were present. Gen. McComb, Gen. Shaer and wife, G. Schermerhorn and wife, Judge Stanton and wife, C. N. Pond, Mrs. Dakin, Mrs. Armitage, Mrs. Col. Fenton, Mrs. Humphrey, Col. Thompson, Col. Cave, Jussen, Major Fulton, Capt. Casey, A. H. Weston, Capt. Burns, Col. Bodine, Judge Gilder sleeve, J. A. Buck, and Col. Wingate. After the toast had been removed, Judge Stanton said that he supposed this would be the last time that the Association would meet with their friends from abroad and it would be in good taste and order to oil the glasses and drink to the health of SIR Henry Halford.


Sir Henry Halford addressed the assemblage as follows: "We are over here for work and not play. Our work is over and I only regret that it has not been successful. But there is no use in crying over spilt milk. We hope again to meet you in another test, and trust that there will be no dissension in these national contests of rifle shooting. I hope that I say when I go back to my country that we will be able to send another British team. I know that I am uttering the sentiments of my Irish friends, when I say that unless we can come over in the guise of a separate Scotch and Irish team, we cannot at all. We must know before leaving this country whether such it to be the case and whether not there is to be dissension upon this question. We are a nation and not three. If you say that as many wish, we can only say that England will take part. In conclusion, I thank you for your courtesy, your reception, your hospitality. It is my pleasure and we will look upon it as a token of good will to my nation—the British nation."

MACKINAC, Mich., Feb. 2, 1877.


And still they come. Another grand ball took place Tuesday night, Jan. 30, at the Fort, this time given by the officers of the garrison. The ballroom was decorated in truly magnificent and luxurious manner, fitted out in regular drawing room style; lounges, easy chairs and comfortable settees were arranged around the walls for the accommodation of the invited guests. The illumination of the room was brilliant. The aristocracy of the Island were well represented. From the beginning of the festivities, at 8 o'clock P.M. until 4 o'clock A.M., the music never ceased; the dancing was only interrupted by the call to supper. If I should describe the display of the well-filled tables and all the tempting viands I would never get through. Never before was so pleased with the arrangements of a ball-party, and I was 10th to leave.


Hardly had I rested my weary limbs, when I was again called to attend a party. This time it was the "boys in blue" it seems, to me. They could not have let such an opportunity slip by. They gave "A hop" on the 1st. and if you like to see a lively dance, you should have witnessed this one. An open table was spread for those who cared to take "just a little lunch." It takes the "boys in blue" to arrange for a party. They cannot be beat. Will you say again, that it is dull on the Island.


I think it would pay the Happy New Year to make us visit. I believe I can safely assure them a full house.


Winter, with all its terrors, seems to have left us. For a fortnight the thermometer has hardly fallen below zero. Finer weather I do not think was ever before experienced on this island, at this time of the year, but I fear the remainder of this month and March will pay us in full for all the nice weather we have been having.


An iceboat has been fitted out and it is waiting to make its trial trip, just as soon as the opportunity presents itself, that is, for a favorable breeze and the freezing over of the many holes, which the thawing weather we have had has made in the ice.


Mr. J. Mcrone lost valuable horse, cutter and the entire outfit, valued at $500, a few days ago. The rig was driven by Mr. L. McKanne, who, accompanied by his wife, was crossing over to the Point, when the horse and everything with it broke through the ice. Mr. McKanne and lady barely escaping with their lives, but the horse and rig were lost.


The Catholic church gave a social in the rooms of the Palmer House, last Monday night. It was well attended, the four rooms being crowded. The whole arrangement was perfect, and the supper was gotten up in good style and deserves all praise.


The members of the Temperance lodge have publicly installed their officers for the next term. I am indebted to men, for the following list of officers:


W. C. T.—W. B. Young.
W. V. T.—Miss Effie Cable.
W. S.—George Lontheimer.
W. A. S.—Miss Jennie Cable.
W. M.—Miss Minnie Chapman.
W. D. M.—Oscar Schoeman.
W. F. S.—Nick Biddle.

W. R. III. S.—Mrs. S. DeBlanne.
W. L. H. S.—Mrs. G. Conrad.
W. I. G.—Miss Emma Bouchard.
W. O. G.—Ernest Nachtigall.

Indian chief discovered their refuge and
sought them in it. At the same moment
an Indian boy attached to John D. Lee's
person discovered the whereabouts of the
girls and the curiosity of the chief and
ran to Lee and informed him. Lee turned at once and fastened to the thicket.
There he found the trembling fugitives
and confronted the chief, who asked him
what he was going to do with them.

Lee responded "They are too old
to live."

The Indian answered "They are too
pretty to kill.

At this juncture the eldest of the two
girls threw herself on Lee's breast, and
wound her arms about his neck and said
"Oh, sir, for God's sake, for your mother's, for your wife's, for your sister's
sake, please let us live! Don't kill us
I can't bear to die. Oh, sir, I'm too
young to be put to death so cruelly! If
you will let me live I promise to be
your faithful servant to tend upon you,
to see to all your wants, to be everything
you could wish poor girl to be, all your
life long. And poor Ella, sir, she is
younger than I. For the love of the
Savior, don't let the Indian do her harm.
Please, sir, as you hope to rest beyond
the grave, let us have our lives preserved."

The Indian, not understanding words
that was said, again asked Lee: "What
shall we do with them?" According to
the testimony of the Indian boy who
stood near, Lee said, not to the Indian
but to the wretched girl whose arms
were locked around his neck: "It is
beyond my power to save you. I am
acting under ORDERS."

At this, the girl who stood apart, named
Ella, drew her sun bonnet down over
her eyes. The Indian chief, overawed by Lee's authority, took humane and
certain aim, and shot her directly
through the forehead. She dropped to
the ground without moan. At the
same moment Lee, untwisting from his neck the arms of his own victim, drew
her head back across his breast and cut
her throat from ear to ear with his hunting knife. Even the Indian turned in
disgust from this callous butchery—a
butchery, however, which Lee persisted
to his death in regarding as a part of his
duty as Latter Day Saint.

Seim Nachmittag kam die Rede zu Schluss auf Handelsoperationen, was Guido veranlasst, seinem Schwager den Plan seines jüngsten Unternehmens auseinander zu setzen. Dieser hörte mit den deutlichen Zeichen des Beifalls rissig-müdig begleitet. Als Guido ihn, hörte seine Frau mit durchbohrendem Blick, durchdringender Spott und bitterer Corn auf seinen leisen Söhnen Lippen kämpften dann sprach er kalt und böhnisch:

"Eine Frau hat in solchen Sinnen ein Wort mitzureden," fiel Herr Paulus ein.

"Zum Teufel auch. ihr Vermögen lebt doch bald auf benz Spiele! Ich sehe es hier unvorherbar Romano benz Gewinn auszusehen, Romano über einem Abgrund in der Schwäche zu halten. uns ihm bald sehen kann zu verargen!"

"Wenn eine Frau Vertrauen lebt in ihrem Mann, so ist es für ihn eine etwas, nicht eine Kat-"

"So, von dem kann? Von benz Groß Herr Grommer, die seine die Warisper spielen, von den alten Söhnen und Bet- Idmeistern, waren Zeit vorüber ist - der ein Persönlicher wenig ist und mit der Zeit fortläuft, denkt sich ich /: das Licht im Leben - gleich zu sein bei der Welt nicht topisch das Rost, als schlimmer die Sicht."

he ascribes his failure to disable the
Kearsarge to the fact that the latter hung
chain cables upon her sides. These
cables were only placed upon her bows,
and had the powder of the Alabama been
in good condition, he presses it as his
opinion that she would have sunk the

Kearsarge in spite of all such protection.
One of the shells of the Alabama which
lodged in the stern-post of the Kearsarge,
did not explode, and saved him this day.
If it had exploded it would undoubtedly

have destroyed Winslow's vessel.

Semmes displayed the greatest coolness

in the handling of his vessel during the

whole of the fight with the Kearsarge,

and when the Alabama was about to
sink he was the last man to leave her.

A sailor named Mars, who had shown
very great bravery during the combat
and who had picked up a shell from the
Kearsarge that fell on the deck of the
Alabama and thrown it overboard—it
exploded before it reached the water—
brought him a life-preserver to Semmes, and

insisted that he should put it on. Sem-
mes refused to do so, and told the sailor
that his lie was worth as much to him
as the admiral's, and that he must put
it on himself. He had in his hands some
valuable papers, among them the bonds
of a number of ships that had been cap-
tured, and these he gave to Mars
directing him to save them at all hazards.
Subsequently some of the officers and
sailors persuaded Semmes to use a life
preserver. Mars was picked up by one
of the boats of the Kearsarge, but jumped
overboard. He was picked up a second
time by another of the Kearsarge's boats
and a second time leaped into the water
and was finally rescued by a French
boat, saving the papers which had been
committed to his care.

Semmes was very strict disciplinarian.
This was especially necessary in the ser-
vice in which the Alabama was engaged.
The line between that kind of service and
piracy was so narrow that but for the
strictest discipline the crew of the con-
federate steamer would have been guilty
of all sorts of excesses. When an Amer-
ican vessel was captured, if it had on
board an American cargo, it was burned.

If the cargo belonged to foreigners, the
captain was made to sign a bond for its
value on the vessel. No officer or mem-
ber of the crew of the Alabama was al-
lowed to take any article from prize.

says that he was once very severely pun-
ished by the captain of the Georgia for
taking from the cabin of a vessel that

amendment. We would have played
into the hands OF the forced resumption
ists if we had suffered defeat OF the
proposition TO repeal the resumption
scheme, rather than win a victory by
mere change of phraseology.


"But, General, why didn't the CON-
mittee frame its bill so as to both repeal
the Resumption act and substitute green
backs for bank notes?"


"That would have been certain defeat
for both propositions. You see large
part of the thirty Republicans and few
of the Democrats who voted to repeal the
resumption scheme are in favor OF Na-
tional Bank currency. On the other
hand, strange as it may seem, there are
some Democrats who favor forced re-
sumption that are dead against bank cur-
rency. The two propositions, therefore,
had to be kept separate to give either the
slightest chance OF success.


"Will Your committee's proposed bill
TO substitute greenbacks for bank notes
pass the House?"


"This is not certain. Every day, how-
ever, increases our strength, for the
people are waking up their Representa-
tives by letters and petitions and per-
suasive appeals, and I think it probable
that the bill will pass this session. This
much will be accomplished at least. We
will force the issue and let the people see
whether their Representatives are for
greenbacks or banking currency in time
for the nominations and elections for
Congress next year."


"Did the Republicans who voted for
the repeal bill stand firmly by your
eyes; it wipes it out entirely and does
not leave vestige?"


"Not all OF them. Mills Gardner, of
this State, did splendid work for the bill,
and deserves the thanks OF his constitu-
ents. There were at least seven Repub-
licans who voted for the bill who wanted
it beaten. These men came near making
the bill ridiculous by voting for the
Wood amendment, which was only de-
feated by one vote. This amendment
proposed TO pay all laborers in gold on
the first day of January, 1879, and the
bill itself proposes to prevent resump-
tion that day."


The bill, then, as it passed the House,
defeats Sherman's resumption scheme?


THE BILL IN THE SENATE.


"What show does the bill stand in the
Senate, General?"


"It is now IN the hands of the Com-
mittee on Finance, of which Morrill, OF
Vermont, is chairman. There are nine
Senators ON this committee. Morrill,
Dawes OF Massachusetts, Herman of New
York, and Bayard of Delaware are set
down as opposed to the bill; Ferry OF
Michigan, Jones of Nevada, Voorhees, OF
Indiana, and Wallace OF Pennsylvania,
are said TO favor it, as it comes from the
House, and Allison, of Iowa, holds the
balance OF power. It will only get out
OF the committee with amendments, and
the character OF these depends upon Al-
lison's views. Two amendments are pro-
posed that will probably be reported
with the bill to the Senate. One pro-
poses to limit the amount of greenbacks
to be issued to the present volume OF
$314,000,000, and fixes the date for re-
sumption some time beyond January
1879. The other provides "that the
banks shall provide redemption fund
from the income OF their government
bonds, and that the greenbacks, after re-
demption, may be re-issued."


"Can the bill pass the Senate,
General?"


"I think it can. I have here a list of
Senators that has been carefully prepared
by the friends of the measure." The
General took from his pocket book a
piece of paper and called the roll.


The following Democrats are opposed
to the bill: Barham and Eaton, OF Con-
necticut; Randolph and McPherson, OF
New Jersey; Herman, OF New York;
Bayard and Salisbury, of Delaware; one
from Maryland; Hill, of Georgia, and
Lamar, of Mississippi. Total, 10. The
remainder of the Democratic Senators
will vote for the bill. The following Re-
publicans are known to be for the bill:
Cameron, of Pennsylvania, Strong, Fer-
ry, Osley, Davis, Ingalls, Plumb,
Dorsey, Spencer, Patterson, Conover,
Jones and Booth. It is thought that
Matthews, Kirkwood, Windom, McMillan
and Wright will vote for the bill.
Without the doubtful ones the bill will
have thirty-eight votes for it in the
Senate as it comes from the House."


THE SILVER QUESTION.


"What is the condition of the Silver
Bill passed by the House?"


"It is in the hands of the Senate
Finance Committee, and will be reported
to the Senate after the recess with two
amendments. One proposes to let the
Government buy silver bullion at the
market price and give the Government
the benefit of the seigniorage, AND the
other proposes to limit the amount of sil-
ver coined by the Government TO not
more than four millions and not less than
two millions per month. The last amend-
ment will be defeated in the Senate."


MATTHEWS RESOLUTION.


"Doesn't Matthews' concurrent resolu-
tion come up before the Silver Bill?"

All the arrangements were completed Saturday night and on Sunday morning, as above indicated, Dr. Norris and friends were promptly on the ground and after waiting the usual time customary on such occasions returned to city. Mr. Bagwell's failure to be on hand promptly was caused, it is asserted, by his having slept a few minutes later than he intended and was otherwise slightly delayed. He endeavored, however, to make up for lost time by driving rapidly to the place appointed for the meeting.

The immediate friends of the principals have since yesterday held several consultations for the purpose of determining what is the proper thing to do under the circumstances reached, but it is intimated that Dr. Norris' friends will not consent to a second meeting on the ground that in appearing on the ground at the time appointed he has not fully vindicated his position. What Mr. Bagwell's friends have decided upon is not yet known.

As already indicated, both parties are well known here. Mr. Bagwell is a Virginian by birth and relative of the Wise family. His brother, General Bagwell, was quite prominent in Virginia politics. Mr. Bagwell came to Baltimore several years ago, and was received in society circles and joined the leading clubs. He is a handsome man of thirty three, of good dresser and generally. His business connections have been with a large clothing house. He is said to be quick tempered and hot blooded. Dr. Norris is a young physician of standing. His father, Somerville Norris, is a well known and wealthy citizen, who resides in an elegant suburban mansion. Dr. Norris is also of good address and recognized leader in fashionable circles.

Our county, or rather the territory embraced in it, became county in 1798. It was no doubt overrun, and partially settled, by land speculators, surveyors and migratory hunters, long before that period. Old records show that various entries were made in 1780, and surveys made as early as 1782-3, and patents issued between 1784 and 1785 for large bodies of land, lying between Green and Ohio rivers. Most of these lands were obtained under settlement pre-emptions, and Virginia land warrants, and are described as lying in Jefferson, Nelson and Hardin counties.

A large portion of the land obtained under the Virginia land warrants were located and patented in the name of wealthy Virginians, at a very early period, and not being settled (or assigned) were lost sight of by subsequent locators, and the consequence was, that the whole territory was shingled over some two or three deep and the actual settlers frequently bought their lands three or four times, as different claimants made their appearance, whilst others, in gaining a lawsuit, abandoned their farms and removed to States and territories where they could get Congress lands, the title to which was deemed indisputable. No people perhaps upon the face of the earth were ever so cursed with land litigations as the people of Kentucky have been, all growing out of defect in the laws of Virginia, regulating the location of lands at the close of the revolution, the market was glutted with Virginia military and treasury land warrants. The rich lands of Kentucky lay open for immense land speculations, but marauding Indians were too numerous to have those lands regularly sectioned, and speculators could not wait. The Virginia Legislature provided a mode of locating lands by entry. Any man, or company of men, could go to the surveyor's office and have entered in the surveyor's book of entries any quantity of land, the law requiring that the calls of the entries should be so special, as to give subsequent locators notice of the boundaries so entered. Had judges, lawyers, or even intelligent surveyors, made these entries, perhaps a moiety of them might have proved good; but it turned out to be, that no man was so great fool as to be thought incompetent, to make an entry of land. The consequence was, that every man who had courage to brave the danger or could be hired or taken in as partner, was dispatched to the wilds of Kentucky, to make land entries. These speculators, or agents, proceeded in something like the following manner: For their own protection and comfort two or more would band together and roam deep into the forest, and finding what they considered a notorious object, they would make out like the following memorandum to be entered in the Surveyor's book:

"John Doe enters ten thousand acres of land as follows—beginning at sycamore marked with the letters J. D., standing on branch and near a deer lick, supposed to be a branch of Muddy creek, which is a branch of Rough creek, and to run from said tree east and north for quantity—7th May, 1782."

"Richard Roe enters ten thousand acres of land, to lie on the east side of John Doe's entry, of this date, &c &c." making in all, some half dozen entries calling to adjoin each other. These speculators, with certificates in their pockets, return to the settlements, awaiting more peaceful times to survey their lands and obtain patents; but in the meantime subsequent locators have commenced at the mouth of Muddy creek, a notorious natural object, and make large entries, covering all the lands of Roe, Doe, &c. The patents are obtained from the latter entries, but Doe, &c, flourish their older entries to innocent ignorant settlers. They buy, but how they fare when the younger entries, but older patents, are tested in court, may be learned by various cases reported in Hardin & Bibb's reports.

CATHEDRAL, NEWARK—THE REMAINS RE-

MOVED TO BALTIMORE.


The first ceremony in the obsequies of His Grace
Most Reverend James Roosevelt Bayley, Archbishop
of Baltimore and Primate of America, took place at
half-past seven o'clock yesterday morning at St. Pat-
rick's Cathedral, Newark, N. J. Within the sacred
auditorium were gathered immense numbers of people,
representing all parts of the State of New Jersey.
Promptly half-past a procession of between
sixty and seventy priests, including Bishop Corrigan,
Bishop Dibbon (Archbishop Bayley's successor), and
Bishop McQuade, moved into the church and took posi-
tions in the sanctuary, the grand organ meanwhile
playing the anthem, "De Profundis."


At on the night preceding, the remains of the Arch-
bishop, clothed in the gorgeous vestments of his
ecclesiastical rank, and reposing in open casket,
were exposed to full view of the congregation, the
white-mitred head being elevated that the face
could be plainly seen from all parts of the Cathedral.
When the hour for beginning the services had arrived,
part of the vast building was used to ventilation,
so that ere long a number of persons were overcome
by the stifling and had to be removed.


SERVICES.
The services for the body of the dead prelate were
impressive to the extreme, and were begun by
the celebrant, Bishop of New York, the Very Rev.
Q. H. Doane, D.D., being assistant
priest; Rev. Fathers Cody and Leonard, honorary
and sub-deacon, and Rev. Joseph N. Flynn, for
ceremonies. The chanted music was the plain music
of Müller's. Professor William A.
Schmidt presided at the organ.


There was but relative of the Archbishop pres-
ent—his niece, Mrs. Bernard N. Shanley. Her tribute
to the memory of the deceased prelate was a beautiful
pillow of excelsior, in the centre of which, worked in
purple buds, were the words, "My Dear Uncle."


Among the noted citizens present were Chancellor
Theodore Runyon, Cortlandt Parker, and a large num-
ber of Protestant society including lawyers, journalists,
doctors, merchants and others.


TAKING A LAST LOOK.

custom, on the part of friends and relatives of
taking a last look at the features of the dead, took
place. The clergy filed round the casket and took
a last look at the dead Archbishop. Next came in
groups the heavily draped Sisters of Charity. These
passed round the casket and after a hasty glance at the
cold and lifeless form of their old friend and brother in
Christ glided lightly into the sacristy. The congregation
next slowly filed around the casket.

Der General Ord überbrückte Seile beschichtlich eines gewissen unmöglichen Übergangs über den Rio Grande mit der merkantilen Weise miteinander verbunden, und viele machte bittere Angriffe auf die ausländische Regierung. Viele Angriffe haben den gelandeten Softe belogen, der Regierung und den Vertretern der auswärtigen Mächte ein Vorhaben zu überblicken, welches sich über die Grundlage und den Zweck des fraglichen Gesetzes erteilt.

Alexander and His Father.


Lucy Hooper in Philadelphia.


In the dearth of any positively startling Parisian news, a little gossip from an European capital may not be unwelcome. I recently had the pleasure of being presented to a charming American lady who has resided for some years past in Russia, and who told me a good deal respecting matters at St. Petersburg. From her I gained the impression that the Emperor Alexander must be the most accomplished sovereign in Europe, as well as one of the most winning of men—grave, gentle, kind hearted, and of the most exquisite distinction of manners. And kings and princes are by no means always refined and accomplished gentlemen, as witness the past; but I say no more. Still, such glamour doth hedge about royalty.


The emperor is said to have great dislike to form and ceremonial, and to be occasionally bothered by our Ministers in that respect. The story goes that some years ago one of our newly accredited envoys arrived at the Palace one day, crammed to the throat with speech. Admitted to the presence of Royalty, the man commenced asking him some questions about our country, but was tremendously interrupted. "One moment, your Majesty—one moment!" cried the new envoy, spreading his fingers fanwise before the Czar's face to check any further outflow of words. The good-natured sovereign smiled and subsided into silence, and our envoy, keeping his eye sternly upon him to keep him quiet, after the fashion adopted with unruly dogs, first drew forth and wiped his spectacles, and then produced a thick roll of manuscript from his coat tail pocket, which he forthwith proceeded to read. Time passed on, and to this eloquent Minister and his successors there succeeded still another, who, in his turn, sought audience of the Czar. His Majesty uttered few words of ceremonious greeting, bowed, and waited with resignation for the customary speech. It did not come—merely a courteous reply to his own remark. Again the Czar said something and looked expectant. "Your Majesty will pardon me, then," said the new Minister. "I have come merely to present my credentials, and have no intention of making speech." "Thank God!" cried the Emperor, springing from his seat and clasping his visitor's hand with joy.


The Emperor Nicholas was very different from the present Czar. He was sovereign of the olden type, magnificent, grandiose, and despotic. One story of his reign sounds like the romantic adventures of Buckingham or of Louis XIV. He was passionately in love with a beautiful Russian lady who was residing in Paris. He wished to summon her to St. Petersburg, but to do so would be to fatally compromise her reputation. The stratagem to which he resorted can only be compared to that of the Duke of Buckingham when he closed the ports of England in order that the bark whose sole freight was the diamond shoulder knot of Anne of Austria might reach unmolested the shores of France. He issued an order that every Russian residing in Paris should return home at once. Of course this proceeding gave rise to the widest rumors of an impending war with France, business was unsettled, men were ruined, etc., but the Czar's purpose had been achieved.


He was a man of very quick temper, and on one occasion was stung by an absurd contretemps into a tremendous outburst of passion one Easter morning. On that day it is the custom for the Czar to go forth from his palace, and, embracing the first man whom he meets, who is almost invariably the sentinel at the palace gate, he exclaims "Christ is arisen!" to which the reply is: "He is risen indeed!" uttered with great manifestations of joy. So on this particular morning forth sailed the Czar, kissed the sentinel on both cheeks, according to the custom, and uttered the invariable exclamation. "Christ is arisen!" "So it is said," answered the soldier, in a thoroughly stolid way. The man was a Mohammedan from one of the Tartar provinces of the Empire. The wrath of the Czar was unbounded, and since that day the orthodoxy of the sentinel who is to guard the palace on Easter Sunday is always very carefully ascertained beforehand. My informant was warm in her praises of the Czarwitch, whom she describes as a model husband and father, devoted to his pretty wife, whose side he scarcely leaves, and setting in every way an example of conjugal tenderness to his future subjects. The other sons of the Czar are inclined to be wild, even our old friend and admiration, Alexis, whose divorced wife, I am told, was recently married to a German noble, and is now residing in Berlin. I hear that our present Minister, Mr. BOXER, is as popular at St. Petersburg as he was at Constantinople; he recently passed through Paris, and I caught a glimpse of him from afar, but had no opportunity of conversing with him respecting his experiences of the Northern Land.


One more anecdote of an American Minister at the Court of St. Petersburg, and I have done. Years ago, during the reign of the Emperor Nicholas, it was when my informant first went to reside in Russia, she said, there was sent from our government as envoy a statesman of the good old-fashioned stamp. On being admitted to the presence of the splendid sovereign, he instantly fell upon his knees. Nicholas looked at him for a moment with supreme disdain. "Arise, Mr. X," he said, "I am neither your sovereign nor your God—why should you kneel?"
